passages.title: The Old Market Square · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
The old market square stands between the bus station and the river road. It is a wide paved area with a clock tower in the centre, four covered seating areas and a line of small shops along its northern edge. A public noticeboard beside the clock tower displays market hours, cleaning dates and community announcements. Two rubbish bins stand beside the seating area, and a drinking-water tap is located near the bus stop. On weekday mornings, sellers place baskets of fruit and vegetables near the entrances.

A narrow path runs from the western gate to the river road. People who use wheelchairs can enter the square through a level ramp at the southern gate, although the path near the flower stall becomes crowded at lunchtime. The square is busiest on Saturday mornings, when families visit the market and musicians sometimes perform near the clock tower.

The town office has prepared a visitor map showing the entrances, toilets, seating areas and bus stops. The map does not show every temporary stall because their positions change from week to week. It is intended to help visitors find basic facilities, not to promise that every path will remain clear throughout the day. The square is a shared public place, and its appearance changes as sellers, visitors and cleaners use it.

passages.title: The Student Radio Project · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
In August, students at Riverbank School helped the community radio station prepare a weekly programme for local families. The project began when the station asked the school to make short announcements about library events, health services and changes to bus times. Twelve students volunteered, and a teacher helped them plan the first recording session.

At the beginning, the students wrote long announcements and read them quickly. The station manager explained that listeners needed time to understand dates, addresses and instructions. The group then divided each announcement into shorter sentences and repeated important times once. They also asked the library and bus office to check the information before recording it. The first programme was broadcast on Friday at six in the evening. A printed schedule was placed at the school gate for people who did not listen to the radio.

After four weeks, the station received nine messages from listeners. Six asked for more information about library activities, while three requested a slower reading speed. The students changed the programme order and added a short pause between topics. They did not survey every listener, so the messages cannot represent the views of the whole community. Still, the project taught students that clear communication requires accurate information, suitable language and attention to the audience. The station invited the group to continue for another month.

passages.title: The Mapmaker’s Promise · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
Every afternoon, Dina visited her aunt's small map shop after school. The shop was crowded with rolled charts, old travel guides and boxes of coloured pencils. Her aunt made maps for walking groups and local history projects. Dina enjoyed drawing roads, but she disliked checking names and distances because the work seemed slow.

One day, a visitor asked for a map showing the safest walking route to the village clinic. Dina quickly marked the shortest road and handed over the paper. Her aunt looked at it carefully. The route crossed a bridge that had been closed for repairs. Dina felt embarrassed when the visitor explained that she had almost used the map the previous week. Her aunt did not scold her. Instead, she asked Dina to visit the road with a notebook and check each crossing, sign and temporary barrier.

Dina returned the next afternoon with new notes. She had found a longer route with a level pavement and a clear crossing near the clinic. She also wrote the date of the inspection at the bottom of the map. Her aunt explained that a map is not simply a picture of a place; it is a promise that the information has been checked for the person who will use it. Dina began to understand why careful details mattered. The new map took longer to finish, but she was proud that it could help someone make a safer choice. From then on, she treated every name and route as something that deserved attention.

passages.title: Preparing a Safe Field Interview · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
A short field interview can help students learn how people use a public service. Before leaving school, choose one clear question, such as how visitors find the community library. Ask the teacher to approve the plan and prepare a notebook, two pens and a school identification card. Students should work in pairs and remain in the agreed public area.

First, introduce yourselves and explain the school project in one or two sentences. Ask whether the person has time to answer a few questions. If the person says no, thank them and move away. Next, ask the prepared question and listen without interrupting. Write down the main points rather than trying to record every word. Do not ask for private information such as a home address, phone number or account details. If you want to record a voice, ask for clear permission before turning on the device. Do not publish a person's name or photograph without permission.

After the interview, thank the participant and check that your notes are readable. Back at school, compare the answers with those from other participants and explain how many people took part. A small interview group can offer useful examples, but it cannot represent every visitor. Students should report the limits of their sample and avoid presenting one person's view as the opinion of the whole community.

passages.title: Why Repair Cafés Matter · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
Community repair cafés give people a place to learn how to maintain everyday objects instead of throwing them away immediately. At a typical event, volunteers with practical experience help visitors inspect a loose chair, a torn bag or a bicycle with a simple problem. The visitor remains involved in the repair, so the event is also a learning activity.

These cafés can offer three benefits. They may extend the useful life of objects, reduce the amount of material sent to waste facilities and help neighbours share skills. They can also make repair feel less intimidating because visitors can ask questions while working. A local group may begin with one monthly session in a library or community hall, using donated tools and a clear safety policy. Items that require specialist knowledge should be referred to qualified repair services. A sign at each table can explain which tasks are suitable for volunteers and which require a trained technician.

However, repair cafés cannot solve every waste problem. Some products are difficult to open, spare parts may be unavailable and electrical faults can be unsafe for volunteers. Attendance figures alone do not show how much waste was prevented, because an item might have been repaired elsewhere or replaced later. Organisers should record the types of items inspected, the repairs completed and the cases referred to professionals. A repair café is best understood as one useful part of a wider approach to responsible consumption. Its value lies in practical learning and shared responsibility, not in a claim that every object can or should be repaired.

passages.title: A Public Bus Pilot · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
The town transport office tested a new bus route for eight weeks between the railway station, the health centre and two residential areas. The pilot used one small bus on weekdays and a larger vehicle on Saturday mornings. Staff recorded passenger numbers at each stop, arrival times and comments submitted through paper forms. The aim was to understand whether the route connected places that residents often needed to visit.

During the pilot, the bus carried an average of 74 passenger trips each weekday. This number counts trips, not individual people, because some passengers used the service more than once. The health-centre stop had the highest number of recorded boardings. The office did not measure whether residents stopped using private vehicles or whether town-wide traffic changed. On rainy afternoons, the bus was sometimes delayed near the market road. The transport office received 32 feedback forms: 21 respondents asked for an earlier first service, while 11 requested a later evening bus. The forms were voluntary, so they may not represent all passengers.

The pilot also took place during a school holiday, when normal travel patterns may have changed. The office has not yet compared travel times with other routes or measured whether residents stopped using private vehicles. The office concluded that the route was used and that the health-centre connection was important to many respondents. It plans to repeat the measurements during a regular school term and publish the method used to count passenger trips. The early figures can guide further planning, but they are not enough to prove that the new route has reduced traffic across the town.
